before.abstract_text: Risk limits on dealer positions concern the largest magnitude reached before a review horizon ends, rather than the position at its endpoint. We compare historical and conditional quantile forecasts of sampled absolute-position peaks for an FX market maker and weekly primary-dealer position aggregates. Simple historical rules prove difficult to beat. At the shorter horizon, long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8% and 16.6% in the previously reported later and earlier windows. Its later advantage survives a delayed adaptive coverage adjustment (ACI). Before correction, however, regression breaches more frequently, while its ranking against a shorter-history rolling rule changes across periods. After stronger regularization, regression still loses 34 of 48 additional-panel comparisons. We formalize the known-floor target and apply a classical endpoint-to-peak bound under explicit assumptions. The results support joint validation of accuracy, breach behavior, and stability across reference rules, periods, and related series. A controlled simulation rejects a universal narrow-regime explanation, while aggregation and the overlapping backcast further qualify the empirical pattern.

after.abstract_text: Peak-position limits concern the largest absolute inventory reached before a review ends, making completed path labels and the observed current position central to forecasting. We compare historical and conditional quantile reports for an FX market maker and weekly primary-dealer position aggregates, using matched histories and update schedules. Simple historical rules remain demanding benchmarks across frequencies, position categories and reference choices. At the shorter horizon, long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8% and 16.6% in the previously reported later and earlier windows. A post hoc history-to-horizon coordinate organizes simulation gains, and a new simulation passes its short-history and long-history prediction screens. Real-record learning curves partly support the predicted first cutpoints, while left censoring, large-history reversals and failures of universal simplification qualify that pattern. For limit managers, these findings motivate matching historical information before assessing conditional forecasts jointly on score, breaches and stability, with history length guiding evaluation.
